claims.text: The baseline material is a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element HEA.
The baseline HEA is homogeneous and has only minor inherent compositional fluctuations.
Cu or Zr can serve as the low-density element in the proposed lightweight-HEA intervention.
A slight increase in the selected element's concentration triggers nanoscale chemical fluctuations.
The resulting nanoscale chemical fluctuations promote formation of a stable protective oxide or passivation layer.
The nanoscale chemical fluctuations provide dislocation-pinning centers.
A continuous protective oxide or passivation film improves corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Dislocation barriers generated by the compositional fluctuations increase mechanical strength.
Slight addition of the selected element concurrently improves strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the baseline HEA.
Increasing the selected element beyond an optimal concentration causes phase segregation.
Phase segregation impedes formation of a protective oxide layer.
Phase segregation disrupts the proposed dislocation-pinning strengthening mechanism.
The property response to increasing addition is nonmonotonic, with initial improvement followed by deterioration at higher concentrations.
The beneficial mechanism ceases to hold above the concentration threshold for significant segregation and detrimental oxide formation.
A controlled composition series should include a no-addition baseline, a sample near the predicted optimum, and multiple samples at higher additions.

The hypothesis is falsified if slight addition fails to improve both mechanical strength and corrosion or oxidation resistance, or if higher additions do not produce the predicted segregation-associated decline.
